dataset.name: Heating effects on pyrogenic organic matter mass loss and temperature in a sand matrix in a lab setting from 2022
description: This dataset contains data associated with the preprint “A laboratory method for simulating the effects of subsequent fires on pyrogenic organic matter at different exposure depths in a sand matrix” (https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.07.30.605814), which has been accepted for publication in the International Journal of Wildland Fire. The dataset was generated to investigate the effects of subsequent fires on preexisting pyrogenic organic matter (PyOM) at different soil depths. Specifically, we designed a laboratory method to simulate soil heating from above, applying realistic heat flux profiles (High, Low, Control) derived from jack pine (Pinus banksiana Lamb.) log burns. Using a cone calorimeter, these profiles were applied to buried jack pine PyOM (produced at 350°C) in a sand matrix pyrocosm to examine PyOM mass loss at different depths (surface, 1 cm, 5 cm). Each treatment (e.g., High heat flux at 1 cm depth) was applied once to five replicates in a pyrocosm.

The dataset includes mass loss fraction of PyOM and time-series temperature profiles (measured with type K thermocouples). Additionally, calibration datasets for high and low heat flux profiles are provided, including programmed heat flux profile data and three sets of calibration results. All datasets are in .csv format and were analyzed in R using code found at https://github.com/MengmengLuo/Reburning-pyrogenic-organic-matter-A-laboratory-method-for-dosing-dynamic-heat-fluxes-from-above.

This dataset supports research on PyOM transformations during subsequent fires, and methodological advancements in simulating soil heating. It can be used to explore fire-induced PyOM alterations across different fire intensities and soil depths.

measurementTechnique:
Detailed methods are available in the preprint:
Luo, M., Yedinak, K., Bourne, K., Whitman, T., 2024. A laboratory method for simulating the effects of subsequent fires on pyrogenic organic matter at different exposure depths in a sand matrix. bioRxiv 2024.07.30.605814. doi:10.1101/2024.07.30.605814.
The paper has been accepted for publication in the International Journal of Wildland Fire. The following steps provide additional details about the uploaded datasets.

We used jack pine log burns to establish high and low heat flux profiles. Heat flux data were collected from direct measurements using water-cooled sensors placed below burning logs on the surface of a sand bed. Characteristic heat flux profiles were generated by tracing the trend of the measured profiles and smoothing out oscillations.
The high and low heat flux profiles used in this study were obtained from an ongoing project at the Forest Products Laboratory. We selected these two profiles because they were generated to be representative of logs burning in realistic jack pine stand fires and together are expected to reflect different fire effects. The high and low heat flux profiles are reported in the data files under the columns titled “Programmed_Heat_Flux” or “Heat_Flux_Setpoint.”

Jack pine PyOM samples were produced at 350°C using a modified muffle furnace under an argon atmosphere. For each fire simulation, 1 g samples of PyOM were mixed with 8 g of sand with 5 replicates and buried at depths of surface, 1 cm, or 5 cm in a pyrocosm containing ashed and washed quartz sand.
The “PyOM_mass_loss” file contains data on the fractional PyOM mass loss for each heat flux profile and depth combination. The total mass loss was calculated by measuring the pyrocosm’s mass before and after the treatment burn. The mass loss was then divided by the original PyOM sample mass in the pyrocosm (which is ~5 g) to obtain the mass loss fraction. For the control treatments, samples were buried at different depths and then dug out without burning, so the mass loss fraction was reported as zero.

The high and low heat flux profiles were programmed into a cone calorimeter with LabView software. Temperature was measured and recorded at the top and bottom of each sample during the entire time of the heat flux exposure. Each heat flux–depth treatment was conducted as an individual burn. Six data files (“lowHF0cm,” “lowHF1cm,” “lowHF5cm,” “highHF0cm,” “highHF1cm,” “highHF5cm”) report the raw data generated from LabView, including complete time-series temperature data for each sample in each treatment.

To ensure the reproducibility of the applied heat flux profiles and minimize calorimeter drift, we also report “highHF_calibration” and “lowHF_calibration.” These files provide time-series data from three calibration experiments conducted on a sand-only blank pyrocosm to confirm that the heat fluxes received by the pyrocosm closely matched the programmed heat fluxes, minimizing potential discrepancies.
